rv.q: Jane Eyre: A Musical is an elegant, tuneful but essentially bang-average affair that boils the source material’s unsettling gothic vision into a boilerplate period love story.
It's just a shame they're working with such flimsy material.

With its excellent cast, outstanding vocals, atmospheric design and timeless romance, Jane Eyre the Musical offers London audiences a passionate and engaging journey into Charlotte Brontë’s unforgettable world.
I’ll concede that I didn’t expect to enjoy this production quite as much as I did.
There is no doubt it has merits, together with some stonking central performances, and is one that musical aficionados won’t want to miss.
Treat it as an opera (it's largely sung through) and grant to it the allowances we do for that oft-overwrought genre and the show works very well indeed, flaws and all.

The lack of emphasis on this first-person narration, so key to Brontë’s implicit act of feminism, is unfortunate, and the piece lacks an obvious female voice, making some of the social commentary shallow rather than timeless.
This musical version of Jane Eyre fares slightly better, but still makes a complex novel a hollow shell of itself.

Yet despite these accomplishments, it never quite captures the emotional sweep of the great romance at its centre, leaving a production that is engaging, but ultimately less heartfelt than it ought to be.
Charlie Burn and Ashley Gilmour share convincingly yearning chemistry as Jane and Mr Rochester.
Although I am not sure that a musical about Jane Eyre was really needed, and there is already an opera by Michael Berkeley, I am pleased to have encountered this particular production.
A transfer to a bigger house is not beyond the realms of possibility for this exciting and fiercely fantastic musical.
This beautifully performed and cleverly staged adaptation show an exceedingly satisfying watch.
This is a fine adaptation that is well worth your time.
Fortunately, in this musical adaptation of ‘Jane Eyre’, the production rightly chooses brevity over detail in an enjoyable UK premiere of this ambitious work.
Filled with soaring ballads of hope and self-reflection, this Jane Eyre is as earnest as its heroine but is light on depth.
Ultimately, there is plenty to admire in this production of Jane Eyre.
This musical acknowledges that tension without ever quite finding a way to resolve it.

However, though adeptly performed by a strong cast in a slick and attractive production, Jane Eyre’s UK premiere at Southwark Playhouse Elephant is held back by a relentlessly bleak tone with very limited levity and without the sense of hope that should be propelling our heroine.
But beyond being overly truncated by its running time, the show's massive flaw is its failure to develop chemistry between the leads.
The musical feels like a speed-run through the book, leaving out many major plot points and condensing everything down to the bare minimum to still tell a cohesive story.
After finally crossing the Atlantic, Caird and Gordon's ‘Jane Eyre: A Musical’ captures Brontë's spirit, even if it doesn’t quite match the novel's force.

cn.t: This earnest musical adaptation of Brontë's classic features strong performances and soaring ballads, but critics find it lacks emotional depth and gothic darkness, with thin characterization and insufficient chemistry between the leads.
